input.question: If Voyager 1 is travelling at a speed of 38,000mph, and if just a small piece of space debris collides with it, wouldn't the probe break or have a major alteration in its course because of the immense speed?
input.ground_truth: The interstellar medium has a very low density, ~10^-4 ions/cm^3, this (roughly) equates to 1cm^3 of matter per cube of space, with a side length of 10,000 km. And most of that material will be individual ions. The chance of hitting anything out there is very remote.

Okay! Imagine Voyager 1 is like a super fast toy car that’s zooming really, really fast—faster than any car on Earth! Now, imagine there’s a tiny pebble in space. If that pebble hits the toy car, you might think, “Oh no! It will break!”

But here’s why it’s not so simple: Space is almost empty, so there aren’t many pebbles around. Also, even though Voyager is super fast, the pebbles are really, really tiny and not very heavy. When a tiny, light pebble hits something moving super fast, it’s like when a tiny feather taps your hand when you’re running—it might feel like a tickle, not a big crash.

But if the pebble is moving really fast too, it could scratch or chip the toy car a little bit. However, Voyager is made very strong to handle space. So, a tiny hit might not break it, but it could maybe change its direction a tiny bit—like if you nudge a rolling ball, it might wobble a little.

So, a tiny space pebble might not break Voyager, but it could make it move a little differently. But because there are so few pebbles in space, this doesn’t happen very often!
